headline: Rich people are spending 13 times more than poor on their kids
author: Julie Z. Weil

paragraphs.text: The gap between how much the rich and the poor spend on their children is widening dramatically.

That’s the conclusion of a new analysis of highly detailed federal data on consumer spending. Orestes P. Hastings, a sociologist at Colorado State University, found that since 1980, the poorest Americans have slightly decreased their spending on their children’s education, care and extracurriculars — while the richest Americans have quadrupled what they spend.

Nearly 50 years ago, Hastings found, rich people spent three times as much as poor people on their children’s care and schooling, and twice as much as middle-income parents. Now, the top 10 percent of earners spend 13 times as much as low-income families and five times as much as the middle 50 percent.

“We attribute a lot of it to the rising pressure,” said Hastings, himself a father who is home-schooling his three children. “It feels more important to the parents for the kids to do well, so they increase their investment in higher quality extracurriculars and schooling. … Families at the top end who have the resources are feeling pressure to dedicate even more of these resources toward their children.”

It’s not that lower-income families don’t feel the same pressure to prepare their children for a highly competitive higher education landscape and uncertain future job market, Hastings added. But at a time of rising costs for necessities such as health care and housing, they simply don’t have the discretionary income to put toward education that rich people do.

“The most surprising was the finding that among the lower-income parents, there is a decline,” said Mariana Amorim, a Washington State University sociologist not involved in the research. “Budgets are more squeezed now than they were in the past. … The price of everything else is going up, so they don’t have the money in their budget.”

Hastings’ analysis of the Bureau of Labor Statistics’s Consumer Expenditure Survey examined only parental spending on child care, education and extracurricular activities, not shorter-term spending on goods like toys and technology.
He found not just that wealthy people spent more money, but that the percentage of their household budget that they devoted to child care and education climbed.

Nina Bandelj, whose recent book “Overinvested” discusses the increased pressure on parents to spend on their children’s development, said companies have worked to persuade rich parents to spend more, including private equity firms that have bought day care chains and gotten into the high-cost children’s sports business.

“With the big parenting economy, all of these things involve a lot of money. Things have become much more expensive both because we value them so much and also because there’s an economy that feeds on parental ideas of what’s best for their children,” she said. “It’s very easy to do that: sell something to a parent who’s exhausted and wants to do the best for their kid.”
For child care, one reason wealthy families are spending more now than in the 1980s is that more mothers are working rather than solely taking care of their young children.

One reason poor families are spending less is that subsidized care has become more widely available. Public preschool is offered in 45 states and covers close to half the 4-year-olds in the U.S. for some part of the day.

Amorim said costlier care often tracks with better care, but not always. Families who aren’t spending anything on child care might have kids enrolled in a great public program, or might be struggling to cobble together a plan.
“Grandma could be great child care … or it could be spotty and unpredictable,” she said. “We just see the amount that’s being spent. We have no measure of quality.”
Hastings said it’s difficult to assess how much unequal spending on children drives future inequality.

“It’s not clear to me,” he said. “Is it really the case that children who go to a more expensive private education or tutoring, are they really going to turn out better than children who don’t? It’s usually parents who already have a lot of resources.”

Amorim said that while spending “probably” matters for children’s futures, “it’s really hard to separate the amount of money” from other benefits that rich parents can often offer, like connections through social networks.
“We can’t say that each dollar buys better outcomes,” she said.
